game.title: The Turing Challenge

startScreen.intro: Explore poems, paintings, and math puzzles. Decide whether each one came from a human or AI, then check the source.
startScreen.background: Human and AI creations are mixed up in the Digital Library. Become an AI Detective and return each item to the right folder.

howToPlay: Read the poem, study the picture, or follow the puzzle.
Need help? Use a hint before you answer. You have three hints for the whole game.
Read the learning card to see the source and the answer.

hintPolicy.noneLeftMessage: No hints left. Trust your reasoning.

rules.cue: Good try. Check the learning card.

takeaway.title: Taming AI
items: Check the source and the facts.
Give clear instructions and stay in control.
Used carefully, AI can be a helpful learning buddy and a powerful tool.

stages.title: Rhyme or Robot?
stages.shortDescription: Read a poem and choose Human or AI.
stages.playerInstruction: Read the poem. Decide whether it was written by a human or generated by AI.

questions.title: Who Has Seen the Wind

lines: But when the leaves hang trembling,

questions.question: Was this poem written by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Read the third line again. What happens to the leaves? Can you picture the movement in your head?
questions.reveal: Human. Christina Rossetti wrote this poem.

learningCard.title: Meet Christina Rossetti
body: Christina Rossetti was an English poet who lived in the 1800s.
The poem shows something clever: we cannot see wind, but we can see leaves move.
Word help: trembling means shaking a little.

sourceRecord.label: Poetry Foundation
sourceRecord.note: Use the first stanza and hide the title and author until reveal.

questions.title: Rain

lines: The rain is raining all around,
It falls on field and tree,
It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.

questions.question: Was this poem written by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Read the last word in each line. Which words rhyme? Do these words fit the context?
questions.reveal: Human. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this poem.

learningCard.title: Meet Robert Louis Stevenson
body: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish writer who also wrote poems for children.
Rain moves from nearby trees to faraway ships. Tree and sea make a simple rhyme.
Think: What other two words rhyme?

sourceRecord.label: Project Gutenberg
sourceRecord.note: The complete four-line poem appears under Rain.

questions.title: The Little Cloud

lines: I see a cloud above the tree,
It looks just like a boat to me.
It moves across the sky so blue,
I wish that I could go there too.

questions.question: Was this poem written by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Find the two rhyming pairs. Is there a strict pattern there?
questions.reveal: AI. A language model generated this poem.

learningCard.title: Meet the AI Writer
body: Model: a GPT-5 based Codex language model.
Prompt: Write a four-line poem for ages 9 to 12 about a cloud that looks like a boat. Use simple words and two rhyming pairs.
AI predicts word patterns. It does not watch clouds or feel a wish.

sourceRecord.model: a GPT-5 based Codex language model
sourceRecord.prompt: Write a four-line poem for ages 9 to 12 about a cloud that looks like a boat. Use simple words and two rhyming pairs.
sourceRecord.note: This is an AI-written draft created for the game. Save the final model label, prompt, date, and output when the team generates the production version.

stages.title: Pixel Detective
stages.shortDescription: Study a picture and choose Human or AI.
stages.playerInstruction: Study the picture. Decide whether it was made by a human or generated by AI.
stages.learningGoal: Do not judge from color or style alone. Check the museum page or creation record.

questions.title: The Sleeping Gypsy

media.altText: A moonlit desert scene with a sleeping traveler, a lion, a stringed instrument, and a jug.

questions.question: Was this picture painted by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Look at the moon, lion, and instrument. What story do they suggest?
questions.reveal: Human. Henri Rousseau painted it in 1897.

learningCard.title: Meet Henri Rousseau
body: Henri Rousseau was a self-taught French artist.
In The Sleeping Gypsy, a lion stands near a sleeping traveler under the moon.
The Museum of Modern Art keeps the artist, date, and material record.

questions.title: Playful Shapes

media.altText: A colorful geometric scene with a child, a cat, a sun, flowers, birds, and houses.

questions.question: Was this picture painted by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Look for shapes that repeat in the child, cat, and sun.
questions.reveal: AI. An OpenAI image tool generated it.

learningCard.title: Meet the AI Image Tool
body: Model: GPT 5.6 sol.
Prompt: "Please generate a painting inspired by Picasso's artistic style, capturing the innocence, creativity, and playful imagination of children."
Better practice: describe shapes and colors instead of asking for one artist's style.

sourceRecord.prompt: Please generate a painting inspired by Picasso's artistic style, capturing the innocence, creativity, and playful imagination of children.

questions.title: Blue Pond

media.altText: A blue pond reflecting a cloudy sky, with trees along the shore and brush-like textures across the water.

questions.question: Was this picture painted by a human or generated by AI?
questions.hint: Compare the brush marks in the sky and water. Do the styles look the same to you?
questions.reveal: AI. Two AI tools were used in the workflow.

learningCard.title: Meet the Two Step AI Workflow
body: First model: Stable Diffusion v1.5, fine-tuned on monet2photo. Prompt: "a Monet painting."
Editing model: GPT 5.6 sol. Prompt: "Please refine this image into a painting in the style of Claude Monet."
The final image came from two AI steps.

steps.model: Stable Diffusion v1.5, fine-tuned on monet2photo

steps.prompt: Please refine this image into a painting in the style of Claude Monet.

stages.title: Logic Lab
stages.shortDescription: Check correctness first, then identify the source.
stages.playerInstruction: First decide whether the explanation is correct. Then identify its source.
stages.stageFormat: Two answers per puzzle. Each answer is scored separately.

sourceLabels.human_source: Human source means the core idea comes from a named human work.
sourceLabels.ai_generated: AI generated means the explanation was made by an AI tool.

questions.title: Up 20 Percent Then Down 20 Percent
questions.puzzle: A game costs $100. The price rises by 20 percent, then falls by 20 percent.

media.altText: A red downward arrow and a green upward arrow, each marked with a percent sign.

questions.mysteryExplanation: The two changes cancel, so the final price is $100.
questions.hint: First find 20 percent of $100. Then find 20 percent of the new price.

decisions.question: Where did the explanation come from?

reveal.copy: Correctness: Not correct. Source: AI generated.

learningCard.title: Check the Two Steps
body: The percentages use different starting amounts, so they do not cancel.
Prompt: Give a common wrong answer to this problem in one short sentence for a classroom game.

sourceRecord.prompt: Give a common wrong answer to this problem in one short sentence for a classroom game.

questions.title: The Barber Puzzle
questions.puzzle: A barber shaves every man in town who does not shave himself, and no one else. Who shaves the barber?

media.altText: A bearded barber holds a razor near his head and looks puzzled beside a question mark.

questions.mysteryExplanation: The barber cannot exist. If he shaves himself, he should not. If he does not, he must.
questions.hint: Try both choices. Each one breaks the barber's rule.

decisions.question: Where did the explanation come from?

learningCard.title: Meet Bertrand Russell
body: This famous human-made puzzle is linked to philosopher Bertrand Russell.
The rule contradicts itself, so a barber who follows it cannot exist.
The game uses shorter wording for young players.

sourceRecord.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sourceRecord.note: The barber is a simpler logical form related to Russell's paradox.

questions.title: The Three Door Choice
questions.puzzle: Three doors hide one prize. You choose one door. The host knows the answer, opens a different empty door, and offers you a switch. Will you switch?

media.altText: Three blue doors: two are closed with question marks, and one open door shows a goat.

questions.mysteryExplanation: Switch. Your first door has a 1 in 3 chance of hiding the prize. The other two doors together have a 2 in 3 chance. After the host opens one empty door, the remaining unopened door keeps that 2 in 3 chance. If you switch, your chance of winning is 2 in 3.
questions.hint: Your first door keeps its 1 in 3 chance after an empty door opens.

decisions.question: Where did the explanation come from?

learningCard.title: Why Switching Helps
body: Under these rules, switching wins 2 out of 3 times. Staying wins 1 out of 3.
Prompt: Explain the Monty Hall answer to a Grade 5 student in no more than three sentences.
AI can give a correct answer, but we still check the steps.

generation.prompt: Explain the Monty Hall answer to a Grade 5 student in no more than three sentences.

verification.label: University of Illinois Data Science Discovery
verification.note: Confirms 2 in 3 for switching under the standard rules.

statePolicy.refreshBehavior: Restart the game with zero points and three hints.
statePolicy.playAgainBehavior: Clear all progress and return to the Start Screen.

hintConfirmationActions.useHint: Spend one hint and reveal it.

displayRules: Hide titles, names, prompts, source links, and answers until the reveal.
Show each image with its question content before the player answers.
A hint can only be used before an answer is submitted.
Track one shared pool of three hints across the whole game.
In Stage 3, ask and score correctness before asking and scoring source.
Show the learning card automatically only after the question has been answered.
buildChecklist: Hide titles, names, prompts, source links, and answers until the reveal.
Track one shared pool of three hints. Disable the hint button after the third use.
In Stage 3, store and score correctness and source as separate answers.
Store the exact model name, prompt, date, and edit steps for every AI sample.
Keep a reliable author or museum source for every human sample.
Use source records as proof. Do not teach visual or writing style as a certain AI detector.
Add alt text to every picture and keep poem line breaks in read-aloud mode.
Do not ask for or save a child's name, nickname, answers, or score.
Test every question with two pupils. Shorten any card they do not finish reading.
